The conflict has also altered the medium-term outlook for global natural gas markets.
IEA’s role and oil stock release
Each of the IEA’s 32 Member countries has an obligation to hold  oil stocks  equivalent to at least 90 days of net oil imports and to be ready to collectively respond to severe supply disruptions affecting the global oil market.
On 11 March, IEA Member countries unanimously agreed to take emergency collective action to respond to the major disruptions in oil markets, making 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks available – the largest-ever release coordinated by the Agency.

About 530,000 barrels per day (bpd) used to arrive in Ceyhan via the pipeline until mid-October, of which about half came from the Kurdistan Regional Government's oilfields and the rest from Kirkuk, a disputed province claimed by both the Kurdish region and Iraqi authorities in Baghdad.

U.S.-backed Iraqi forces ousted the group from Mosul in July, after a nine-month campaign supported by Kurdish Peshmerga fighters.

The Department of Defense (DOD) broke ground on the Project Pele transportable microreactor project at Idaho National Laboratory (INL).
The demonstration project is being led by DOD’s Strategic Capabilities Office and could be one of the first advanced reactors to operate in the United States as early as 2026.
Project Pele Breaks Ground
DOD is planning to design, build, and demonstrate a transportable high-temperature gas reactor that will operate at the lab’s Critical Infrastructure Test Range Complex.
The reactor will be manufactured by BWX Technologies and connected to INL’s microgrid producing 1 to 5 megawatts of electrical power.
Project Pele is a whole-of-government effort, with critical expertise provided by the Department of Energy, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, NASA, and the National Nuclear Security Administration.
The reactor is expected to operate for a minimum of three years at the lab and will help demonstrate the use of clean, reliable, and transportable nuclear power to help meet the increasing energy demands at military bases across the country.

The Army Bets $2.2 Billion on Microreactors at Five Bases, With One Due Online by September 2028
* Microgrids Military & Defense News
* Marin Holt
* August 27, 2026
* 0
* 198
* 7 minutes read
Key Facts
* Reactors range from 1 MW to 20 MW and are contractor-owned and contractor-operated
* At least one reactor must be operational by September 30, 2028
The US Army selected five companies on August 26 to build nuclear microreactors at five installations. The agreements are worth up to $2.2 billion through fiscal 2031. The program is called Janus.
Fuel choices differ across the group. Radiant and Antares plan to use HALEU in TRISO form. General Atomics plans uranium zirconium hydride. Jeff Waksman, the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment, leads the effort on the Army side.
The Army frames Janus as energy independence.
A 1 MW to 20 MW generator that runs for years without refueling is a microgrid asset, not a power plant. Diesel gensets and batteries carry most installations through an outage today. Both depend on fuel deliveries or on a short discharge window. A reactor sized to a base changes the resilience math, because the fuel is already on site.
They do not speed up the licensing.
Milestone-based payment protects the money, not the timeline. If Antares, BWXT, General Atomics, Radiant and Westinghouse all slip together, the Army has spent little and gained nothing on schedule. The resilience claim needs a test as well.
